transcript:
Meeting header:
- Date/time: 2026-04-15 10:30 PDT
- Duration: ~72 minutes
- Meeting title: Deployment Isolation & Scaling Runbook - Scrub
- Attendees: Maya Chen (Redwood AE), Omar Ruiz (Redwood SE), Priya Kapoor (Solstice Head of ML Infra), Liam O'Connor (Platform Eng), Dr. Hana Lee (CTO), Evan Mills (SRE), Sofia Martinez (Security)

Summary:
Quick scrub of dedicated vs hosted deployment tradeoffs with emphasis on isolation runbooks, noisy neighbor mitigation, and throughput guarantees. Discussed KV cache prefetching, batching windows, quantization impact on tail latency, and VPC/on-prem networking constraints. Agreed to run sandbox perf tests and share detailed cost/runbook docs.

Topics:
- Isolation models: fencing, GPU tenancy, pod vs node eviction
- Noisy neighbor scenarios and mitigation (cgroup limits, eviction, circuit breakers)
- KV cache: hot-key handling, prefix caching, prefetch windows
- Batching: dynamic vs static windows, cost-latency tradeoffs
- Quantization: 8-bit vs 4-bit impacts on throughput and hallucination rate
- VPC/on-prem: network egress, KMS integration, air-gapped concerns

Quick note on artifacts: Maya referenced a deck and a pilot spreadsheet: https://redwood.app/sales/runbooks/deployment-runbook.pdf and a sandbox perf sheet at https://drive.google.com/sandbox-perf-sheet (customer to be granted access).

Action items (captured verbally during call): see action_items field above.

Transcript body:
[00:00] Maya: ok thanks everyone for joining, we wanted to run through what a runbook looks like when you're deciding between hosted and dedicated for production workloads, especially for latency sensitive endpoints
[00:12] Priya: yeah thanks, we, um, I'm primarily worried about noisy neighbor and how that crops up during peaks, we saw some jitter on our internal GPU clusters last quarter, so that was, that was painful
[00:22] Omar: totally, and just to set expectations, we'll cover the isolation knobs (tenant fencing, dedicated GPU pools, pre-warming), then we'll walk through KV cache strategies and batching windows that keep p99 in check without killing cost
[00:36] Liam: quick question, when you say 'tenant fencing' do you mean hard GPU attribution or soft queueing? we have both in-house workloads and public facing rp services so curious trade-offs
[00:47] Omar: good callout, so in Redwood Dedicated we offer hard fencing (pinned GPU pools) and soft multi-tenant lanes. Hard fencing basically maps a customer's instances to a fixed set of GPUs with guaranteed ratio; soft lanes use scheduling + cgroup caps and rely on runtime QoS for isolation
[01:02] Dr. Hana: and is storage for KV cache local to the GPU node or networked? because our models rely heavily on prefix cache for chat sessions
[01:12] Omar: by default the KV cache is in-node memory (GPU VRAM and host ram for sharded kv), we also have a networked redis-style fallback for very large contexts but that adds tail latency. For Dedicated we can prioritize hot-key placement and keep the most hot-shard local to the GPU to avoid remote hops
[01:30] Evan: when you say "hot-key" how do you handle skews? our traffic is highly spiky and a single user type can dominate requests for short bursts
[01:38] Maya: yeah so we instrument hot-key detection and then proactively prefetch those keys into the local KV region, Omar mentioned a prefetch window -- how long is that window typically?
[01:46] Omar: it depends on your session length distribution, we usually start with a 30–90s prefetch window for chat workloads; it's a heuristic: if a token sequence pattern repeats within that window we keep it warm. For extremely spiky patterns we use a lightweight rate limiter and tail-shed to protect p99s
[02:02] Priya: that tail-shedding concern is big for us. we can't drop requests without graceful fallback. what does graceful degrade look like?
[02:10] Omar: good question. common pattern is layered fallback: 1) try smaller quantized model variant (fast-8bit or 4bit) 2) reduce max tokens and use cached prefix to continue the session 3) route to a lower tier region or burst pool. The runtime supports automatic fallback policies so the app sees continuity even if latency rises
[02:28] Sofia: on the security side, if you do prefetching into dedicated GPU memory, how is encryption and key management handled? we have to keep customer data encrypted at rest and rotated via KMS
[02:38] Maya: Dedicated integrates with your KMS for key wrapping, and we keep cache contents encrypted on host memory using per-tenant keys; we also rotate keys per customer on schedule. we'll share the exact KMS integration notes in the security packet
[02:50] Liam: can you speak to kernel selection and quantization impact? we've seen some 4-bit runs improve throughput but produce more variance on tail latency
[03:00] Omar: yeah quantization is a trade. 8-bit (q8) is often a sweet spot — good throughput improvements with predictable latencies. 4-bit (q4) can give ~1.8–2x throughput vs fp16 but it sometimes increases variance and can change logits leading to slight quality regressions. We also pick kernels based on seq-len and attention pattern; sometimes q4 kernels are slower at short seq-lens due to additional dequant/decompress costs
[03:22] Priya: do you have benchmarks showing p50/p95/p99 for q8 vs q4 on mixed chat workload?
[03:28] Maya: yes, we have a sandbox benchmark. Omar, can you summarize the last run?
[03:32] Omar: sure — in our last customer run with 2k rps baseline and 500 concurrent sessions, q8 kept p99 under 420ms for 2k tokens sequence distribution; q4 had lower average latency but p99 occasionally spiked to 1.2s under hotspot conditions. we'll share the perf sheet, note that the numbers depend a lot on batching behavior and KV hit rate
[03:52] Evan: batching behavior, right — what's the recommendation for batching windows when you need <200ms p95?
[03:58] Omar: if your p95 target is <200ms you should keep batching window tight (3–10ms) and prefer continuous batching where the runtime flushes based on latency SLOs not just batch fullness. Redwood's runtime supports dynamic batching: it adapts window based on observed latency and util. That said you pay in throughput efficiency if windows are tiny
[04:16] Dr. Hana: could you explain continuous batching vs fixed slots? our infra team tends to think in fixed slot sizes because it's simpler operationally
[04:25] Omar: fixed slots are easier but less efficient. continuous batching aggregates requests as they arrive up to a short window and can merge partial KV caches; fixed slotting schedules on time boundaries and can lead to wasted cycles when load is low. For Dedicated we can tune the continuous batching aggressiveness per model and route
[04:40] Liam: trying to map to costs: if we go dedicated with pinned GPUs, what's the utilization delta required to make it cost-effective vs hosted?
[04:50] Maya: typical breakeven depends heavily on rps and average tokens per request. As a ballpark, for steady 24/7 high throughput workloads where GPUs are above ~45–55% utilization, Dedicated often becomes economical due to lower per-token costs and reserved capacity pricing. We'll send the cost model spreadsheet with scenarios
[05:06] Priya: one of our constraints is network egress and VPC peering. if we choose Private (VPC) deployment, how does that affect failover and cross-region routing?
[05:16] Omar: Private deployments support private peering and can keep inference in-region; failover is policy-driven — we can configure multi-region fallback but that requires cross-region replication of KV or graceful recomputation. Note replication increases cost and complexity. For critical low-latency endpoints we prefer regional Dedicated with local KV placement
[05:34] Sofia: air-gapped option — do you support on-prem appliance deployments for regulated data?
[05:40] Maya: yes, Redwood Private can be delivered as customer-managed control plane + on-prem inference nodes. In that mode you get full network isolation, local KMS/HSM integration, and restricted telemetry. It does add ops burden — we provide an ops playbook and runbooks for upgrades
[05:56] Evan: circling back to noisy neighbor mitigation — beyond fencing what are runtime guardrails?
[06:02] Omar: several: adaptive cgroup CPU/GPU caps, request-level circuit breakers per tenant, per-model qps policing, and per-GPU kernel time slicing. Also, we maintain a priority queue for critical endpoints with preemption capabilities so lower priority batches can be paused
[06:18] Priya: any examples of preemption causing client-visible latency spikes?
[06:22] Omar: in our experience preemption is rarely visible if you have fallbacks configured — the runtime will attempt a model variant switch or reduce max tokens. Without fallbacks, preemption could introduce jitter, yes
[06:33] Liam: how do you validate noisy neighbor protections in staging? can we run synthetic attack tests?
[06:39] Omar: absolutely; we recommend a soak test that includes noisy neighbor injection — run synthetic workloads that hammer KV hotkeys, burst token generation, and saturate GPU memory. We can provide a test harness; that will give you a clear picture of p95/p99 under adversarial load
[06:53] Priya: about KV eviction — how deterministic is the eviction policy? we need session affinity for some medical workflows
[07:00] Omar: eviction is configurable. Default is LRU-ish with hot-key protection; for session affinity we can pin user session keys to a shard and avoid eviction for X minutes. There's a memory vs persistence trade though; pinned sessions occupy more RAM so you should only pin where needed
[07:14] Dr. Hana: for compliance we also need audit trails — who accessed which cache entries, when — is that logged?
[07:20] Maya: yes audit logs capture KV access events at a coarse level, and Dedicated/Private can include more verbose tracing. We'll include sample log snippets in the security packet
[07:28] Sofia: on RBAC and SSO — can we scope access per model/route? we want least privilege for dev vs prod keys
[07:35] Maya: yes, per-route RBAC and token scoping are supported; tokens can be restricted to models, capacity pools, and time windows. Also supports SAML SSO with SCIM provisioning for accounts
[07:46] Evan: a practical question: for a mid-month traffic spike, is there autoscaling that quickly adds capacity to dedicated pools or do we rely on burst capacity?
[07:56] Omar: Dedicated has autoscaling policies but they work within your reserved capacity envelope; we also offer burst capacity (paid) to handle short spikes beyond reserved commit. Autoscaling latencies depend on probe times and image startup; we recommend warm buffers for sub-minute scale-up needs
[08:12] Priya: warm buffers meaning maintain a small warm pool of idle workers?
[08:16] Omar: exactly. keep a small number of pre-warmed workers to absorb sudden spikes. The runtime also supports fast prep of new kernels for popular model variants reducing cold-starts
[08:26] Maya: wanted to show a brief snippet from the runbook on run-to-failure vs graceful degrade — (Maya shares link in chat)
[08:32] [screen share audio noise] Maya: so this is the policy flow: normal -> stressed -> degraded -> failover. thresholds are configurable by token rate and p99 latent breakpoints
[08:44] Liam: who on our side needs access to the perf sheet? Priya and Evan I guess?
[08:48] Priya: yes, Priya and Evan will own that. I'll share session distributions and prompt corpus by EOD 4/18
[08:54] Omar: perfect. we'll prepare two sandbox scenarios: 1) steady throughput, 2) spiky hotkey attack, and will capture p50/p95/p99 and token cost
[09:02] Dr. Hana: curious about fallback quality regressions — do you have an eval harness to compare q8 vs q4 differences on our prompt sets?
[09:09] Omar: yes Redwood Optimize includes a quality monitoring pipeline; we can run A/B evals on your prompts and provide BLEU/ROUGE-ish metrics plus human review notes for edge cases. That will help decide if q4 is acceptable for certain routes
[09:24] Priya: can we talk briefly about telemetry retention for Private vs Hosted? we have data retention limits for logs in our org
[09:30] Maya: Hosted retains metrics at default window, but for enterprise we offer configurable retention windows and can route logs to your SIEM in Private deployments. We'll include retention options in the security packet
[09:42] Sofia: do you provide SOC2 + ISO docs for Dedicated specifically?
[09:46] Maya: yes we have SOC 2 Type II and ISO 27001, plus a dedicated responsibilities matrix for Dedicated and Private deployments. I'll attach those docs
[09:55] Evan: one last ops detail: how do upgrades work for Dedicated GPU nodes without affecting live traffic?
[10:02] Omar: we do rolling upgrades with traffic draining and pre-warming; for zero-downtime we coordinate canary instances and fallback routing. In Private/on-prem it's customer-managed but we provide a step-by-step ops playbook
[10:16] Priya: ok this is helpful. to recap, sounds like: 1) Redwood to share runbook + pricing and perf sheet, 2) Solstice share prompt corpus and distributions, 3) Redwood + Solstice schedule sandbox perf tests week of 4/27. correct?
[10:30] Maya: yep that's accurate. Omar anything to add?
[10:33] Omar: just that we'll include a noisy neighbor injection script and a sample quantization eval in the perf runs
[10:39] Dr. Hana: thanks all, I might bring a dev from infra next time to go deeper on the VPC peering specifics
[10:45] Maya: great, we'll follow up in email with calendar invites and artifacts. thanks everyone

End of transcript.
